newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - Kashmir revolt ruins birds' winter haven.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Kashmir revolt ruins birds' winter haven.

text.p: The sounds of exploding hand grenades and booming guns have silenced the cackle of wild geese in India's Kashmir region.

A seven-year-old separatist rebellion, which police say has claimed at least 20,000 lives in the troubled Himalayan valley, has sparked environmental degradation that has robbed hundreds of thousands of birds of a home in its green wetlands.
The violence first scared away some 300,000 Hindus from the Moslem-majority state of Jammu and Kashmir after guerrillas launched a separatist revolt in 1990.

Ornithologists have now discovered that shrinking wetlands, ruined by years of government neglect during the rebellion, have translated into a sharp fall in the number of migratory birds that find a winter home every year in the valley.
NUMBER OF BIRDS NEARLY HALVED SINCE 1990

"There is almost a 50 percent decrease in migration of birds because during the last seven years, all the sanctuaries, wetland reserves and other swamp areas -- the natural habitat for these migratory birds -- have faced degeneration," ornithologist Kuldeep Singh Jamwal told Reuters in Srinagar, the state's summer capital.
Immediately after the onset of autumn every year, flock upon flock of honking, squawking birds fly into the valley.
Many species of waterfowl, duck and geese migrate from Central Asia and northern Europe to Kashmir after flying over some of the world's highest mountains.
The first of the birds arrive in August, when garganeys, a species of small duck, come to Kashmir. The last birds to arrive are the mallards, wild ducks that fly in from Siberia.
But things have changed because administrators preoccupied with dealing with the armed rebellion have paid little attention to protecting the birds' natural habitats.

"Negligence of the authorities, excessive siltation and rampant encroachments (on natural wetlands) by villagers have reduced these aquatic habitats to mere water holes, leaving no space for our guest birds," Jamwal said.
The birds inhabit 16 swamps and wetlands at altitudes ranging from 1,583 to 1,635 metres (5,192-5,363 feet).

Most of the wetland reserves are situated on a 45-km (28-mile) stretch near Wular Lake, some 50 km (30 miles) from Srinagar in northern Kashmir on the banks of the river Jhelum, which cuts across the valley.

"Our wetland reserves have shrunk to such an extent that these cannot fully accommodate immigrant flocks," said a senior wildlife official. "That is why some of the birds bypass the valley and others have stopped winter stays in Kashmir."
"According to our survey, in a few reserves, over one-fourth of the entire population of the immigrant flocks has abandoned their winter stay," said M.S Bacha, a wildlife warden.
SOME WETLANDS COMPLETELY DESTROYED
The Hygam wetland reserve, 45 km (28 miles) north of Srinagar, has been completely destroyed.
"In 1988, Hygam's wintering geese population was 40,000. Now only 200 to 500 geese frequent the reserve," Jamwal said.
"Over 22 species were regularly coming to the valley in winter. Today, the winter tally of species has declined to 14."
Exotic birds like whooper swans, curlews, sandhill cranes, barheaded geese and purple coots have completely stopped migrating to Kashmir, ornithologists say.
The honking call of the barheaded goose remains only a memory for Kashmiris, who watch members of the species bypass their valley and fly to the remote Ladakh plateau.
Hokersar, Kashmir's most famous wetland reserve, was once home to up to 150,000 birds in mid-November, when mists enshroud the snowy Pir Panjal mountain range nearby.
According to a recent survey, the number of birds in this reserve has declined to 60,000.
"We are losing our traditional heritage. We could not prove good hosts for these birds," said Rajiv Singh, a teacher and bird-watcher.
The state Wild Life Department has taken steps to educate people living near sanctuaries and wetland reserves on the importance of saving the reserves, a department spokesman said.
"There are chances of revival of these wetland reserves," the spokesman said.
Some others say things may never be the same again.
"I fear the honking and calling by greylags (wild geese) in unison may forever disappear in our valley," Jamwal said.
